Is this the single-worst interface of all time? 
I have yet to see a worse one.

If you can find a way the play the games, it's exactly what I expected and that's cool, but good luck getting a game to actually open, much less exit when you're finished. Confusing layouts, insanely terrible menus, wildly inconsistent functions for buttons. 
Capcom is lucky poor UX isn't punishable with prison time.

Absolutely awful experience, avoid at all costs.

I really wanted to like Capcom Arcade Stadium — the idea of having a collection of classic arcade titles all in one place sounds great on paper. Unfortunately, the execution leaves a lot to be desired.

The emulation feels off, with noticeable input lag and inconsistent performance across different games. Even on solid hardware, frame pacing and slowdown issues pop up far too often. The CRT scan line filters are also underwhelming — even at 1440p, they look artificial and don’t capture the authentic arcade look.

It honestly comes across as another quick cash grab rather than a carefully crafted preservation effort. I’ve built PCs with better emulation setups in the past that run these same games smoother and with more accurate visuals.

Not worth my time here. Sorry, Capcom — this one just doesn’t hold up.

Pre-lim Review starts here:
So, normally I would wait until I got the 100% of cheevos in a game before reviewing it and also waiting for the Dust to settle, updates-wise (I never really liked games changing while I'm playing them, unless that's part of the game of course), but there's a cheevo that requires you to play a game 1000 times sooooo....I'mma just post a preliminary review because I see a fair amount of negative reviews that refer to stuff that seems to have been fixed in updates.
Date: 6/27/2022
Preface: Got the 3 Pack Bundle because I actually knew I wanted to play enough of a percentage of the games in the bundle to warrant not just buying things individually. Might have been a mistake due to some sort of "Time Limited Bonus" you can get after you buy a game for the stadium, but oh well, I hate IRL Time Limited stuff in games anyway. Players should own their games, not the other way around, ya know?

Intro: Right away, my first impression was "that's a lot of introduction/tutorial popups for a glorified emulator library program" There's got to be a better way to present this info, ya know? Anyway, the menuing isn't the worst, but to those who are more used to basic no-nonsense stuff for old games, this kind of "Wow, look at all this cool stuff we hired a graphic design to model and everything" menu is probably a turn off. I can understand why. "Why are you wasting my CPU power on this?," they're apt to say. (I say it too, honestly. I would have much prefered a simpler interface without such excess.) But I guess this was to try to hype it up, or something? Anyway, my rig can cope so no big deal for me.

Next, I went to get to the game I actually wanted to play first: Bionic Commando. After going through what should have been just a listbox but was instead a bit more, I found the game and started it. Immediately, more Tutorial Pop-Ups. Really, people? There has to be a better way. At least they stop showing up after they're done. Anyway, I get through the mess of pop-ups and find....oh. Oh dear. It's one of [b]those[/b] arcade simulators eh? The kind that tries to simulate playing on an actual cab by messing with your view of the game in ways including: wasting CPU/GPU by adding a 3D cabinet as a border for the game screen, distorting your view of the game by making the game screen be viewed from an angle instead of straight on, and having screen distortion at extreme angles instead of actually making the game look good. Now, this gimmick is obviously a nuisance and there are other reviews that call it out as such. [b]HOWEVER,[/b] if you go into the display settings, you can change the display to actually look like a game and not a simulation of a game. Change the "Frame" to "2D", change the "Display Size" to "Normal", and change the "Display Filter" to...well, I went with "Type B" but this is the aesthetics setting so it's not like I have a clue what it "should" be. The net result is that this looks like a good emulator instead of a bad simulator. Problem solved. (I will write a guide if there isn't one already.)

Next, a different (and old) review mentioned that there was no way to set the game speed before starting. But in the current version, when I select a game and then go to "Game Settings", there is in fact a setting there to set the game speed there. So it looks like the Devs are actually addressing the issues so far.

Another old review said that, at least in the case of Street Fighter II, the six action buttons weren't even mapped. In the current version though, that seems to have been addressed. I went into the Controller Settings and found that buttons were set up in what seemed like a pretty reasonable configuration and all the stuff that should be mapped actually was mapped. I also found that you can map buttons as you please, even unmapping some functions (like the speed) entirely if you don't like them (there's literally an Erase function to simply remove the mapped button from a function, which is actually something a lot of games lack entirely). There's even an initially unmapped pair of actions for the Light/Medium/Heavy Punches/Kicks at the same time, though I have no idea where that would go on a controller. I should mention, though, that I was using a normal, non-arcade controller when I did this since I haven't committed to investing in an arcade controller. Yet. So, there's a chance the devs haven't set up the game to work nicely with Arcade Controllers. If/when I get one, I'll update this review with my findings.

All ya'll saying this game has microtransactions don't know what MTX even is. MTX would be charging you per play, or for play time. Or for wallpapers you don't even want. (BTW, Arcades INVENTED microtransactions, and they still did it better/more fairly than modern games. Getting good meant not paying as much.) But here, for each DLC, you are literally paying for free play of a game forever. An entire game, which was (usually) well liked when it came out, and isn't some trashy mini-game.

And the 'nickel'd and dimed to death' gripe some reviews have? I'm sorry, but what about the people who literally just wanted 1 game out of the whole collection? Or the people who only like shmups/fighters/etc? And all the people who can't afford to get all the games at once? Why should they suffer? And if you want all the games, there's literally a button on the store page to buy them all. Even the cheevos are set up nicely for that, since they're not tied to any specific game in the collection.

BUT! Capcom or whoever decided how to sell it all gets big points off in my book for not using Steam's Bundle feature, instead opting for the Package method. Even though Capcom or whoever doesn't offer any Bundle Discounts for the content, it's still better for consumers if you make sure to not offer any purchasing methods that could result in buyers paying for something they already own and won't get a second copy of. I'm gonna give the Capcom Arcade Stadium a passing score for one reason and one reason only: the games are good, they run well and it's a decent bang for your buck overall. That's three things. 
If you just want to boot up the arcade classics from your childhood or explore a world before your times in case you're a younger peruser, then go ahead and enjoy. I did too, don't get me wrong, but when looking at the whole picture there's quite a lot of stuff that i have issues with. 

I wasn't a fan of how there's no explanation anywhere of what differenciates the japanese and international ROM of each game. And on one hand i can understand why, as most descriptions would boil down to either "the japanese version was a wreck and we had to fix up so much shit that there's not enough space here to list it all up" or "we have made this game worse for the west for absolutely no reason" and that's not the most flattering way to present a product you've charged money for, but on the other hand... who gives a shit? These games are 30 years old at their youngest, you can put on your historian hat for a second and be honest about your own work, Capcom. 

And since we're on the topic of history and what-have-you... would it have killed you to include any kind of old promotional material in the collection? Flyers, magazine ads, commercials, that kinda stuff. I know this is the Capcom Arcade STADIUM and not the Arcade Museum like i erroneusly called it in one of my earlier reviews for the games here included, but after playing Atari 50 every kind of game collection out there seems so low effort in comparison. I'm not asking for in-depth developer interviews or exclusive factoids or 3D renders of the arcade cabinets with the accurate stickers attached on, just the bare minimum. I know you're keeping all this stuff stored in some hard drive already, it's an afternoon's work. Come the fuck on guys. You don't even have to translate the japanese stuff if that's somehow too much effort over the same games you've been reselling for the 20th time. 

Since there's no flyers and anything of the sort, the games are explained to you through digital manuals, digital manuals that suck ass if i might add. I've found them to occasionally be incomplete or even incorrect, for example in Captain Commando its mentioned nowhere that you can sprint by double tapping the movement input, and in Forgotten Worlds there's an explanation for a mega attack that's not actually doable in the game, and if i dig more i doubt i won't find more examples like these. Default inputs sometimes wil need to be remapped, as they can be counterintuitive or clunky, like in the case of Dynasty Wars or, once again, Forgotten Worlds. 

Challenge runs are a genuinely neat inclusion, unfortunately i suck at videogames so just getting at the credits is enough of a challenge for me, but if you're looking for a way to spice up your playthroughs and to swing your big gamer dick in front of the world it's somethign you can do. You can also edit the dip switch settings of each game if you want a more personalized experience, another thing i liked there.

But i'd hate to end this technically positive review on a positive note, so here's why save states in the Capcom Arcade Stadium are weird and stupid: first off, all games share a limited amount of save slots, which is less than the total amount of games included, different versions notwithstanding, secondly there's no quick button to reload a save state, thirdly saving each still takes a few seconds which depending on how you wanna use them can be annoying, fourthly i wish there was a way to turn off rewinds altogether because it's an unrelated feature i've only used once that's clearly meant to replace the practicality of save states but absolutely does not.

[b](This review is for both Arcade Stadium Editions available as of the original date of publishing this review, so the body of text is repeated for my review of Capcom Arcade Stadium 2.)[/b]

Capcom Arcade Stadium, both 1 and 2, are solid collections of games that I am not disappointed in owning. I love to play arcade games, but have a difficult time mastering them. With these collections, I can play a wide variety of games - bullet hells, fighting games, platformers, Puyo Puyo-likes, Tetris-likes, Match 3s - and master my timing and skills in these games which I still fare horribly at.

Having a rewind/slow-mo/fast-forward feature is very much appreciated, one that I also loved in SEGA Genesis and Mega Drive Classics (which I still own). I'm not very good at Street Fighter, for instance, but I can better practice the Special Moves in slow motion (I have no idea how to execute them properly yet, and I've been playing SF for about three years now). I can also rewind, if a move I make is not well executed.

Some games I don't really like, such as Darkstalkers (although I appreciated Felicia's innocent, playful personality), but I'll almost always play a Mega Man game, and I know that there are two in these collections!

[i]PLEASE NOTE: One con about this title is that it uses The Enigma Protector, a type of DRM Capcom is using on older titles in place of Denuvo Anti-Tamper. However, I would not be too worried about it, as it is not super aggressive and can be defeated with anti-DRM tools if necessary - let me stress for legal reasons that I am NOT recommending this and do not endorse piracy or cheating, but if you're only playing offline AND not sharing the software, then it can be done - but even with Enigma in the game, all it really is meant to do is prevent cheating in the ranks, so I say leave it be.[/i]

That being said, I do believe that this game is a nice selection of games, with a great presentation and quality of life features that make these games more enjoyable in a modern setting. I do still find it frustrating that the invincibility setting is locked behind a paywall, preventing players from trying out a way to play the games in a new way and testing out different ideas in a less time consuming way, which is why I can only assume that's the reason why they offered it for free in the second collection.
Getting back to this collection, I do find it has many interesting games, such as Strider, the arcade version of Ghouls and Ghosts, and some other classics that I don't believe were ported to English and brought overseas. There's beat a game, beat a game on the hardest setting, beat any game 10 times, beat any game on the hardest setting 10 times, start a game 1000 times, play for 100 hours, get max Capso Rank (the score you get when you exit a game). It's all very unengaging and boring and tedious for no real gain, and doesn't encourage you to try out every game. Usually, I achievement hunt games to see everything the Devs have to offer, but here, you can somewhat realistically get 100% completion from just the free game included in the base download. It's a shame really since there are plenty of fun games to try out. I do reccommend getting this when it's on sale, as you can buy all games in the bundle for less than the the specific games you do want. If you do that (and just cheat the achievements, if you actually care about them), then you should have a fun time.

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆ A Fantastic Arcade Collection — But Missing Some Key Regional Versions

Capcom Arcade Stadium is a wonderful tribute to one of the greatest arcade legacies in gaming history. The presentation is slick, the emulation is smooth, and the selection of titles covers an impressive range of genres — from shooters and beat ’em ups to classic action and platformers. It’s pure nostalgia, beautifully packaged for modern systems, and the ability to adjust difficulty, add rewind, and use save states makes replaying these classics more fun than ever.

That said, there’s one frustrating issue that holds it back from being perfect: the inconsistent inclusion of regional versions. Some games are missing their English-language releases, while others are missing their Japanese versions, and this inconsistency can be annoying for players who care about historical accuracy or just want to play the version they grew up with.

What’s especially disappointing is that certain games — like Mercs and Armored Warriors, for example — are Japanese-only in this collection, even though they were officially released in English in the West decades ago. There’s really no reason these versions shouldn’t be included, especially since Capcom has always been good about preserving their multilingual history in other releases.

Despite that, Capcom Arcade Stadium remains a must-own for arcade fans. The gameplay quality is top-notch, the customization options are great, and the collection as a whole is bursting with energy and nostalgia. With just a bit more attention to regional version variety, it could easily be the definitive Capcom arcade experience.

🎮 9/10 – A stellar celebration of Capcom’s arcade history that deserves full regional support to truly shine.

Tested the setup with the free copy of base Street Fighter II.  This is really good emulation.  Expect to get your butt whipped in some of these games, even if you set the difficulty to easiest. Basically there are 3 tiers of menus, after you load up the arcade selection screen.  One on the arcade selection screen, one after you select an arcade (this is where you get game settings for things like speed and difficulty), and one after you hit A after selecting an arcade, which launches the game - this is where you need to be to rebind controls.  Has a rewind feature and save states.  I don't notice any input lag.  Got the 3 bundle set for ~$25CDN on a 50% off sale.  Lots of coop games, both same time and take turns.  Going to have a lot of fun with this.

[h1]Retro Games, modern prices[/h1]

Capcom Arcade Stadium has been a.. "controversial" release to say the least, and I feel most of the reasons cited for it are a tad undeserving. The collection uses Mame, a free and open source arcade emulator, the absolute best in class, which is reflected here. (minus one 1942 logo bug that Mame fixed but is still broke here) This is huge, as not only did Capcom PROPERLY FOLLOW THE LICENSE OF THIS ONE (looking at you final burn alpha), but it shows that the efforts of the Mame team are now even recognized by companies, and that free and open source emulation is here to stay, and is welcomed by the systems they emulate (baring you Nintendo) 

The emulation as I stated, is perfect, all the dip switch settings are available to you, tate mode for those vertical games, and the sound is now perfect too (Mame at the time of the switch version did not have sound cores that could be used commercially, so Capcom made their own, really bad ones, they have since replaced them with the new Mame ones, and they sound fantastic.) Input lag is non existent and it even has default controls for both controllers and arcade sticks!

The fronted is powered by re engine, and its alright, its smooth, the games show attract videos, and unlike Mame, navigating the options doesn't make you wanna blow your own head off with an awful outdated ui. My main gripe is you cannot make the machines look as they actually did, no original artwork, no custom models, just generic bland trash.

So why the hate? If the emulation is rock solid, supports the community, and is improving with updates, why do 64% of Steam users not recommend the game? I've complied the main points I've seen, and will try to answer them.

[b] -You can emulate them for free![/b]

You can also pirate the collection too if you felt like it, just because Mame exists (which need I remind this collection uses.) doesn't mean official releases are simply just not allowed to exist. Mame is in a grey area legally, while other emulators can throw up the "We tell everyone to only use their dumped games and we wont help pirates!" shield, Mame cant. Mame is the one emulator where you HAVE to pirate the games, usually the whole damn 50gb of it if you want to ensure it works. I am absolutely for the free sharing of roms, in an age of DRM and abandonware, so many games would be lost to time if not for roms, but getting free roms through piracy does not make an official collection have less value.

[b]-Its too expensive! Why cant they sell them individually?[/b]

I agree, 50 bones for some roms and an emulator they didn't make is steep as hell, and while Capcom has stated they will sell them individually, (the price of each game was listed as $2.50 on Steam before Capcom hid them) there's zero reason why it should not have been a day 1 option.

[b]-No online![/b]

1. Remote play together
2. I'm sorry but, how often are you really going to use it? The online in these collections ALWAYS dies instantly. Check out that Street Fighter collection, or the Samurai Showdown collection, the Beat em Up collection. Or that time players said they wouldn't buy an XBLA port of Golden Axe unless it had online, which on launch, had 2 total players online. All dead onlines that players begged to have in. I get there are people would genuinely use it once or twice, but its just not worth it. If you want online, use Fightcade, Retroarch Netplay, or Steam Remote Play Together. All great options (with fightcade having that rollback netcode everyone loves.)

[b]-Its not really free![/b]

N-no shit? They advertised 1943 as being free. get your head on right.

The primary complaints about this collection really boil down to "price too high" which while a fair point, do not automatically make the collection itself bad, Capcom making the game free really fucked this up as any brainlet can download it, get upset its not free, and say it sucks, which is just absolutely unfair.
